summary: DMARC lets Domain Owners request aggregate reports from receivers. This Standards Track document defines those reports as an XML document with extensible elements, sent to the destination declared in DNS. It obsoletes RFC 7489.

eli5.summary: Mail receivers send the domain owner a summary, like a monthly tally of how many letters looked real or fake.

questions: what is the rua tag in dmarc
how does dmarc verify external report destinations
subtitle: The XML daily summary that mail receivers send to a domain owner about who is sending mail in its name.

tldr.problem: A domain owner who publishes a DMARC policy needs to see which servers send mail claiming to be from its domain and whether that mail passes authentication, or it cannot safely tighten its policy.
tldr.mechanism: Mail receivers send an XML aggregate report, normally covering one UTC day, to the address in the policy's rua tag. Each report covers one DMARC Policy Domain and lists record elements with sending IP, message counts and SPF and DKIM results.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9990 is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 7489 together with RFC 9989 and RFC 9991. It adds structured report identifiers, extension points and a required DKIM selector.

today: RFC 9990 is a Proposed Standard from May 2026 and obsoletes RFC 7489, whose DMARC specification was split into three documents: RFC 9989, this one and RFC 9991. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Aggregate Reports Exist
sections.content:
DMARC lets a Domain Owner ask Mail Receivers for reports. Aggregate reports show which IP addresses send on the owner's behalf and give some insight into whether the volume looks legitimate. They expose the DMARC policy and the outcome of SPF and DKIM validation.

The RFC says this visibility is critical to running accurate authentication deployments. When owners can see the effect of their policies, they are better willing and able to use quarantine and reject policies.

Reports are meant to be daily or more frequent. They cover messages that passed DMARC authentication as well as those that did not, counted over all messages received, even if other filters later block delivery.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school asking every post office to send a tally of letters that carried its name. The tally shows which letters were real and which were fakes, so the school knows what is going on.

sections.title: The Report Format
sections.content:
A report is an XML document whose root element is feedback, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dmarc-2.0. The first-level elements must appear in this order: an optional version (which must be 1.0), report_metadata, policy_published, an optional extension and one or more record elements. The format is defined by an XML Schema in Appendix A.

report_metadata names the reporting organization, a contact email, a unique report_id and the date_range. The range is given in seconds since the epoch, should not overlap with other reports, and typically covers a single UTC day starting at 0000UTC. policy_published records the policy the receiver found, including p, sp, np, adkim, aspf and a discovery_method of psl or treewalk.

Each record holds a row (the source_ip, a count and the policy_evaluated disposition with DKIM and SPF alignment results), the identifiers (header_from, and optionally envelope_from and envelope_to) and the auth_results with raw DKIM and SPF results. An evaluator that gets a document in the wrong format SHOULD discard it.

If alignment fails and the applied policy differs from the published one, the reason element MUST be included. Its type is one of local_policy, mailing_list, other, policy_test_mode or trusted_forwarder.
sections.eli5: The report is a form with the same boxes every time: who is reporting, what dates, which rules the school published, and then a list of which sender sent how many letters and whether each passed the checks.

sections.title: One Report per Policy Domain
sections.content:
A report MUST contain data for only one DMARC Policy Domain and one policy configuration. It can still hold several RFC5322.From domains, each with its own record.

The RFC's example has example.com, foo.example.com and bar.example.com. Explicit DMARC Policy Records exist for example.com and bar.example.com, but not for foo.example.com, which relies on example.com's policy. That gives two reports. One is for bar.example.com with a single record. The other is for example.com with records for example.com and foo.example.com.

Receivers also have to cope with policy changes mid-period. They may send a single report that mixes old and new policy, or several reports for the same period, one per published policy. Report Consumers should expect mixed reports while a new policy propagates.

When a message carries several DKIM signatures, a report SHOULD contain no more than 100 signatures for a given row. They are ranked from a passing signature in strict alignment, then a passing one in relaxed alignment, then any other passing signature, then failing signatures.
sections.eli5: Each tally is only about one school rule set. Buildings that follow the main school's rules go on the main school's tally, and a building with its own rules gets its own.

sections.title: Finding and Delivering Reports
sections.content:
A receiver finds the reporting request when it looks up the DMARC Policy Record for an RFC5322.From domain. The rua tag says where to send feedback. The receiver MUST go through the reporting URIs in order, may ignore malformed ones, and MUST try to deliver to every remaining one, up to its own limits. If a destination is unreachable, it MAY cache the report and retry or discard it. Unless the URI says otherwise, it SHOULD use a secure transport, meaning TLS via SMTP+STARTTLS.

By email, the message follows RFC 5322 and MIME. The XML is attached, SHOULD be compressed with GZIP and uses the media type application/gzip (or text/xml if uncompressed). The attachment filename has the form receiver!policy-domain!begin!end[!unique-id].xml.gz. A re-sent report MUST reuse the same filename, so the recipient can overwrite or discard the copy.

The Subject line MUST follow a fixed pattern naming the policy domain, the submitter and optionally a Report-ID. The Report-ID MUST be unique among reports to the same domain. Mail carrying reports MUST itself pass DMARC with an aligned pass, which reduces the risk of fraudulent reports.

Duplicates are left to the recipient. Options include rejecting with a permfail error, discarding, inspecting timestamps and data, or accepting the data.
sections.eli5: The post office looks at the school's note to see where to send the tally, shrinks it into a small package so it fits, and puts a clear label on the outside so the school can tell if it got the same package twice.

sections.title: Verifying External Destinations
sections.content:
A domain can ask for reports to be sent outside its own Organizational Domain, for example to a service that handles reports for it. Without a check, an attacker could publish a record naming a victim as the destination and then send lots of mail that fails both DKIM and SPF, flooding the victim with reports. So the receiver MUST verify the arrangement first.

It takes the destination host and builds a DNS name by prepending _report._dmarc and then the domain the policy came from. It then queries for a TXT record at that name. At least one record that parses as a DMARC record, with v=DMARC1 first, means the destination agreed. If the name would be too long for DNS, or no valid record is found, the URI MUST be ignored.

In the RFC's example, the policy for blue.example.com names reports@red.example.net, so the receiver queries blue.example.com._report._dmarc.red.example.net. A destination willing to take reports for any domain can publish a wildcard TXT record at *._report._dmarc.example.com. The confirming record may carry its own rua, but it MUST use the same destination host.

A destination overwhelmed by volume can remove the record, though positive caching means the change can take as long as the record's TTL.
sections.eli5: Before mailing a tally to someone else's house, the post office phones that house to ask if they really want it. No answer means no delivery.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content:
The report format has two places for other XML: an extension element after policy_published at file level, and extra elements after auth_results inside a record. Extension elements MUST be in their own XML namespace, and the extension MUST give a URI that defines it, so receivers know how to read the data.

Extensions are optional and any number is allowed. A processor that cannot handle one SHOULD ignore it and move on. The RFC's example uses the made-up elements arc-override and arc-results to show the shape.
sections.eli5: The form has a couple of blank spaces where someone can add new boxes later. If you do not understand a new box, you just skip it.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says aggregate reports hold no personal information: no individual mail addresses, no IP addresses of individuals and no message content. The data is domain-level authentication information. It therefore argues that receivers and owners should have no concerns about sending or receiving them. An owner who cannot receive reports internally can direct them to an external processor.

Two risks remain. Third-party recipients may be able to do traffic analysis and learn metadata about a receiver's traffic. Also, reports sent to a Public Suffix Operator for a Public Suffix Domain can leak information. The RFC separates single-organization suffixes such as .mil, multi-organization suffixes that require DMARC such as .bank, and those that do not, such as .com, where the risk can be significant. To limit this, feedback for a public suffix domain MUST be limited to aggregate reports.
sections.eli5: The tally only counts letters and never says who the people are, so it is safe to share. The only worry is a stranger in the middle seeing patterns in who gets mail.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
Reports are processed automatically, so a malicious report can attack the processor. The archive decompressor and XML parser are at risk of resource exhaustion (a zip bomb or XML bomb). Report data can also be forged, in volume, to influence policy decisions, and a volume attack could stop a Report Receiver accepting genuine reports.

The RFC strongly discourages using extensions to disclose message placement such as Inbox or Spam, because that would teach a malicious party about the receiver's filtering.

Operationally, error fields should be terse and useful. The XML is not readable in bulk, so owners will likely load the data into a dashboard. Once data is extracted and indexed, the raw reports seem to have little value in most situations.
sections.eli5: Anyone can mail a fake or booby-trapped tally, so the school's tools must open the packages carefully and not trust what is inside blindly.
